title: Type Inference
definition: TypeScript's ability to automatically deduce the type of a variable without requiring an explicit type annotation.
simpleExplanation: If you write `let x = 10`, TypeScript isn't stupid. It sees the 10 and says, 'Okay, 10 is a number. Therefore, x must forever be a number.' You don't have to explicitly tell it.
realWorldExample: Hovering over a variable in VS Code that has no explicit type, and seeing that TS perfectly understood it was a `string[]` based on how you initialized it.
useCases: Keeping code clean and less verbose
Relying on return types from standard functions

basic: Do I need to type every single variable in TypeScript?
intermediate: When does type inference fail and require explicit annotations?
advanced: How does inference work with Array `.map()`?

answers.question: Do I need to type every variable?
answers.answer: No. It is considered an anti-pattern to write `let name: string = 'Alice';`. Because TS infers it perfectly, adding `: string` is just visual clutter. Let inference do the work.

answers.question: When does it fail?
answers.answer: When you declare a variable without giving it an initial value: `let data;`. TS doesn't know what it will be, so it falls back to the dangerous `any` type.
